reading.title: Math Behind the Map
reading.purpose: See how trail maps and hiking guides rely on ratios, rates, and integers to keep travelers on course.
paras: A folded trail map looks like a simple drawing, yet almost every line on it hides a math idea. Before a cartographer prints a park map, each real dimension—such as the length of a ridge or the width of a canyon—must shrink to fit onto a sheet of paper.

To shrink land accurately, mapmakers use a scale ratio, comparing inches on paper to miles on the ground. For example, 1 inch to 2 miles forms a clean proportion with 3 inches to 6 miles, because both pairs compare distances in the same way. Every blue line and triangle on the sheet must correspond to a real stream or peak in the park.

Elevation charts add another layer of numbers. Heights above sea level appear as positive values, while desert basins below sea level appear as negative ones; together with zero, these whole numbers form the set of integers. When you compute the climb from -20 feet to 480 feet, you find a total rise of 500 feet.

Hikers also pay attention to pace. Walking speed is a rate, such as two miles per hour, that compares distance and time. Knowing your pace helps you avoid routes that exceed the daylight hours left before sunset. You can check your plan with inverse operations: multiplying speed by time gives distance, and dividing distance by speed undoes that step.

Even trail blazes follow a pattern. Park rangers set the frequency of painted tree markers—how often they appear along a mile—so walkers stay confident at every fork. Good math turns a paper map into a reliable guide.

choices: the steepest slope found along a mountain ridge
how often painted markers appear along a trail
the brightest color rangers paint on a tree trunk
the total number of miles printed on a folded map

qs.q: Why would a hiker divide distance by speed before starting a late-afternoon hike?
choices: To make sure the trip will not take more daylight than remains.
To count how many painted tree markers rangers placed on the trail.
To turn negative elevations below sea level into positive integers.
To shrink the length of a real canyon onto a single sheet of paper.
qs.why: Dividing distance by speed gives travel time, which lets a hiker check whether the route exceeds the remaining daylight.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Desert basins below sea level are harder to map than tall mountain peaks.
Most hikers walk at an exact pace of two miles per hour in national parks.
Rangers paint bright blazes on trees so people do not need paper maps.
Everyday map reading and hiking depend on several core math concepts.
qs.why: Each paragraph shows a different math concept—scale ratios, integers, rates, and frequency—that makes a trail map useful.
